sweep_summary: Herero (here1253) is in the catalog as tonal, deciding source Elderkin 2003 (Nurse & Philippson ch. 29, full text on file, no stress statement). The sweep's single title item, Möhlig 2003 'The prosodological structure of Herero' (FAB 15: 165-180), is a first-hand modern prosodic study; no open copy exists (archive.org 0 hits, HathiTrust search blocked, no DOI), but Google Books snippet view (12 feed queries saved as gb_feed_51-132.xml) yields the key passage of sec. 2.2.2 'Respiratory accent': a primary and a secondary accent exist and 'Words usually bear a main accent on the penultimate syllable' (okuMUna 'to see', omuRIse 'herdsman', oMUre 'tall'), with accent shift onto following demonstratives (okakàMBÈ ngà) and in predicative clauses, and an expressive first-syllable accent that demotes the penultimate demarcation accent to secondary. This refines the catalog (which says no modern source states word stress) and points to recoding tonal -> fixed penultimate-with-tone under the catalog's Bantu convention, but the full text (Möhlig 2003, or Möhlig & Kavari 2008 Reference Grammar pp. 40-79, publisher-PDF only, no preview, not in HathiTrust) should be read first — both priority high. Also re-fetched sources from the migrated AAeO host the open-access Lusekelo 2009 review of Möhlig & Kavari 2008 (silent on stress, tone only) and re-read Brincker 1886 (root-syllable accent, 19th c.). new_statements.reading: The one modern first-hand prosodic study of Herero states a word-level dynamic ('respiratory') accent that usually falls on the penultimate syllable, co-existing with lexical/grammatical H/L tone; there is also a secondary accent, the accent shifts rightward onto a following demonstrative (noun + demonstrative form one accentual word) and in predicative clauses, and an expressive first-syllable accent can demote the penultimate 'demarcation accent' to secondary. This directly fills the catalog's stated gap ('no word-stress rule stated in any reachable modern source') and, under the catalog's convention for penult-stress-plus-tone Bantu languages (Shona, Setswana, Sotho, Lingala), argues for recoding tonal -> fixed penultimate (dominant, 'usually') with tone kept in the tone note. Evidence is snippet-only: 12 Google Books feed snippets (verbatim, no page numbers) — the full text of Möhlig 2003 or of Möhlig & Kavari 2008 pp. 40-79 should be read before a final recode.

sources.note: Herero has a 'respiratory' (dynamic) accent alongside H/L tone: a primary and a secondary accent are distinguished; the main word accent 'usually' falls on the penultimate syllable (okuMUna 'to see', omuRIse 'herdsman', omuHOnge, oMUre 'tall'); the accent shifts rightward when a demonstrative follows the noun (okakàMBÈ ngà, showing the demonstrative is prosodically attached to the noun) and in predicative clauses; an emphatic/expressive accent on the first syllable can degrade the penultimate 'demarcation accent' to secondary rank. sources.citation: Brincker, P. H. 1886. Wörterbuch und kurzgefasste Grammatik des Otji-Hérero. Leipzig: Weigel. Grammar appendix sec. XVIII 'Wortstellung und Accent', item 7a.
sources.quote: 7) a) Der Accent eilt nur in affektierter Rede zur letzten Silbe zum Ende des Satzes hin; in gewöhnlicher Rede kann man denselben nur auf die Grundsilbe eines Wortes legen, wodurch letztere als solche sich kennzeichnet, wie ú-nga-ra, longa, arbeite; Nomen: oma-ú-nga-ri-ro, ovi-úngura, oma-lóngelo ... b) Wörter, in denen sich ka ... befindet, haben den Accent auf dem ka [Translation: The accent moves to the last syllable, toward the end of the sentence, only in affected speech; in ordinary speech it can be placed only on the root syllable of a word, which thereby marks it as such ... b) words containing ka ... carry the accent on the ka]
sources.locator: grammar appendix sec. XVIII item 7a-b ( lines 30991-31000)
sources.note: 19th-century missionary statement: word accent on the root syllable (first stem syllable), final accent only in affected/emphatic speech; agrees with Viehe 1897 (root syllable) and against Kolbe 1883 (generally final). Impressionistic, pre-tonological; not a modern source.

sources.citation: Lusekelo, Amani. 2009. Möhlig & Kavari 2008. Reference Grammar of Herero (Otjiherero) [review]. Afrikanistik-Aegyptologie-Online 2009. doi 10.18716/ojs/aaeo/2009_3535.
sources.quote: The bank of tonemic behaviours in Otjiherero is intensively provided (pp. 40-79). Such behaviours range from distinctive tone patterns, examples the lexical tones H-H -hórá „to ripen‟, H-L -hóra „to remove hair‟ and L-L -hora „be stiff‟ (p.41) to an extra high tone occurring in the language, exemplified by o.mbwá „dog‟ and Ő.mbwá 'it is a dog‟ (p. 45). Moreover, the introduction of pragmatics and language use through intonation and focus into contemporary Bantu grammars by the authors is highly recommendable (pp. 47-50).
sources.note: The review (already the catalog's supporting source) reports only the tone analysis, extra-high tone, intonation and focus of Möhlig & Kavari 2008; it never mentions stress or accent placement, so it is silent on where word accent falls. Re-fetched sources from the migrated OJS host (same 7-page PDF).
